> Para 21:  Conflicts with P 20:  hostility of leftists versus their
> alleged masochism.  More importantly, P 21 rather misses the long period
> of time when economic justice was demanded forcefully but with
> considerable grace and tact by MLK and others.

Good point, but perhaps K. is talking about *today's* leftist rather
than the nonviolent leftists of the early 60's. What puzzles me is that
he seems to be mixing up the politically correct 90's left with the 40's
stalinist leftist types.
See 227 where Ted admits that "it is still far from clear what we mean
by the word "leftist". several surrounding paragraphs reflect the same
disclaimers. In one place he even leaves us the option of "you will have
to judge for yourself". this conciliatory approach is at odds with the
more forceful tone of other parts of the manifesto.

> Para 29:  Where does this line of reasoning extend to?  TK seems to be
> arguing that the scholastic and economic inequalities which were
> maintained for hundreds of years in the US between whites and blacks are
> somehow essential to the maintenance of blackness.

No, he is just debunking the superficial notion of a black culture which
mostly involves making Black folks good little cogs in the machine just
like white folks, only letting them have their rap music & soul food.
Perhaps there are things in genuine traditional *african* culture that
would be more desirable from Ted's point of view.


> The discussion of the "power process" - how much of this is accurate
> sociology, and how much of this is TK projecting what *he* felt about
> being distanced from the Noble Savage by Society onto everyone?

Most of it is the latter. I don't think that's a problem. I didn't read
the Manifesto expecting it to be a highly researched sociological tract
complete with boring surveys, statistics & footnotes. I've seen enough
of those unreadable things. The Manifesto is one writer's
*beliefs/opinions*--- and it is so much better than the abovementioned
dry, pseudo-objective socio-tracts that it reads like a bestseller by
comparison.

> 
> Para 61:  How much of this discussion of mere obedience at work can be
> read in light of what we now know about TK working at a job much like the
> one he's describing here but *working for his brother,* and being
> essentially ordered by his brother to stop treating one of his coworkers
> bizarrely?

Plenty of others have had jobs like that too. McDonalds, data entry,
graphics production. The other major category of work is Sales &
Management, where you have to do more than what you're told: you have to
CARE about the company's goals too. Oh, then there's jobs like nursing,
where you Can't do what you care about, because it's against doctor's
orders. (in my case, it means forcing poor suffering 95-year old
bedridden patients to stay alive & suffer, because of our
pseudo-compassionate "life"-valuing society... oops, I'm digressing.)

> Para 69:  TK should've tried visiting Africa before praising the
> "stoicness" in the face of the risk of disease.  

of course no one wants to die of a disease. I understand that in India
people know they can die from bathing in the polluted Ganges, but they
don't seem to care... the good karma from the holy river outweighs life
& death.

On the other hand, look at our society's fear of death & the lengths we
go to to deny disease. See above par. about nursing & look at how people
will stay at jobs they hate in order to retain insurance.

> 
> Para 73:  Communes have been attempted periodically to escape the
> pressures outlined in this paragraph.  Almost without exception, they've
> failed within a span of a very few years.  (And those communities which
> have succeeded in maintaining their identity base their rejection of
> society less on such mundane topics as who works for whom and why than
> they do on a deeply-held religious faith.)

Do a web search on the Twin Oaks community in Virginia. Twin Oaks has
been around for 30 years. It's a very successful commune and I think the
big appeal is the "work credit" system. People are required to work a
certain number of credits--an hour equals a credit, whether it's
management or dishwashing. This gets rid of hierarcy & inequality. They
can do a variety of chores at a variety of times. This gets rid of the
rigid   9-5 schedule that is so dehumanizing. Also, it's a small
community, so everyone is cooperating w/everyone else rather than
working for a big fat cat boss. 
I think it's a pretty good way of life myself, and I'd be there except
my family wouldn't want to move. 

[discussion of birthrate/anthropolgy snipped. I think these are

REAL point of the manifesto, in my opinion, starts at about par. 111.
"Tech. industrial society cannot be reformed">

> Para 87:  The Motives of Scientists.  I found this section to be
> particularly weak.  I think that again, because of his isolation even
> when he was in an academic setting, he didn't give sufficient weight to
> the notion that there are people who really are just curious, and get a
> great deal of satisfaction from engaging that curiosity.

Here's where the projection is strongest. Don't forget, Ted was a
mathematician who was concerned with the behavior of circles &
lines--not the most interesting field of study.

> Also, I expect TK would suggest that examining the abundance of lead
> isotopes to study the age of the solar system is of no conceivable

> in the early 60's ultimately forced the oil companies and car companies
> to give up on using leaded gasoline because of the public health threat
> posed by lead settling from tailpipes.  It's sort of surprising to see

Yeah, but in general Ted hates science. I'm sure he rightly despises the
Space Program. Which is where we always hear the argument about how pure
science always leads to useful commercial applications. Like Ted cares!

> Para 89:  The last sentence is a criticism of scientists' motives.
> However, those motives are just fine - exactly as TK states them - with a
> number of systems of belief:  being here, now, as Leary would encourage
> us - not focusing on the goal (as TK would urge us to) but on the
> journey.

I think Ted is missing something: the same abstract satisfaction a
scientist gets from solving a problem is what HE gets from doing a
carving (or maybe from making a bomb.)

> They are asking to be able to voice these "broader social implications"
> explicitly.  They recognize that they are now being given an ethical
> agency, and that they need to be able to act on it in the open.

some scientists may have protested unethical things like the H-Bomb, but
if they did, not enough people listened to them. At this point, if 10
scientists protest cloning and even got all the governments to ban it,
there's still another asshole who will do cloning in his basement. How
to prevent runaway science from creating disasters? by SMASHING SCIENCE,
that's how. Smash the Universities, terrorize or kill the scientists ,
destroy the factories and burn the technical books.

Now I'm not saying I would advocate such a thing... but when following
this line of reasoning, one finally understands what was going on in the
Unabomber's head when he sent bombs to universities. After all... that's
where science comes from, isn't it... from institutions of higher
learning. This is why he bombed professors as well as corporate execs. 

All that power process stuff seems to be window dressing to me. When
taking Ted's 1971 essay into account, it seems that what he fears is
runaway science & progress & what it has done and still may do to this
planet. If he hates science, the universities are the logical target.

You can say he is evil, unethical, etc... but illogical he ain't.
